newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. committee calls for anti-personnel mine ban.
newsitem.headline: U.N. committee calls for anti-personnel mine ban.

text.p: A General Assembly committee called on Wednesday for a legally binding international agreement to ban the use, stockpiling, production and transfer of anti-personnel landmines.

The disarmament and international security committee vote on the draft, sponsored by the United States and more than 80 other countries, was 141-0, with 10 abstentions. This assures its endorsement by the assembly at a later date.

Abstaining, mostly on self-defence and national security grounds, were Belarus, China, Cuba, North and South Korea, Israel, Pakistan, Russia, Syria and Turkey. Cuba had proposed an amendment calling for the legitimate rights of states, in particular the right to self-defence, to be taken into account when the proposed agreement was negotiated.
But this was blocked when a motion by the Netherlands, seconded by Germany, to take no action on the amendment was approved by a vote of 95 to 26, with 14 abstentions.

The resolution expressed deep concern that anti-personnel landmines killed or maimed hundreds of people every week. It noted that the landmine crisis continued to worsen, with an estimated two million new ones laid every year while only some 150,000 were cleared last year.
The resolution welcomed various bans, moratoria or other restrictions already placed by some states on anti-personnel mines and urged others to follow suit.

It asked Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali to prepare a report in time for next year's General Assembly session on steps taken to complete an international agreement banning anti-personnel mines as well as on other steps to ban or restrict their use.

When U.S. Ambassador Madeleine Albright introduced the resolution this month, she said an estimated 110 million mines were scattered across more than 70 countries and would claim another 100,000 victims by the start of the new century.
She said even if no more anti-personnel mines were deployed, before those now in place were cleared the "new century will be over -- and so will the six centuries following that."
